corrected_statement: Under prediction (folds not time-ordered), every pair of families is compared on the repeated k-fold substrate (max(user repeats, 10) repeats of K folds, default 10 × 5, units kept whole) by the corrected repeated k-fold t: over the rK paired fold differences d of the primary, se = √((1/(rK) + n₂/n₁)·s²_d), n₂/n₁ the mean per-fold ratio of rows scored to rows fit, t on rK − 1 df, interval mean(d) ± t·se; the versus-baseline verdict uses the same se and df but centers its interval on the difference of the two reported cross-validated scores (for R² the pooled estimate), not on mean(d), and calls 'better' only when the interval clears zero and the gain is at least 0.01. The K(K−1)/2 pairwise intervals are labeled descriptive (not multiplicity-corrected); the family choice is corrected by BBC-CV. The approximate validity of the interval at 10 × 5 is taken from Bouckaert & Frank's 10 × 10 results, not checked here.
source_note: Formula and df verified: CRAN correctR vignette gives Bouckaert & Frank's repeated k-fold form t = mean(x)/√((1/(kr) + n₂/n₁)σ²); Crossref confirms Bouckaert & Frank, PAKDD 2004, LNCS 3056:3-12 (doi 10.1007/978-3-540-24775-3_3). The repo's own excerpt (audit/modeling-sequence-review.json) quotes B&F recommending 10-times 10-fold CV with the corrected test 'for best replicability'; their study is of test replicability and Type I error for classifier accuracy on 10 × 10, not of interval coverage at 10 × 5 or for log loss/R² differences. Nadeau & Bengio's n₂/n₁ correction was derived for random subsampling (a heuristic, no unbiased variance estimator exists). So the code follows the cited formula, but the regime (10 × 5, proper scores, interval coverage) is extrapolated. Could not fetch the B&F PDF directly (waikato links 410).
note: The named test (passes) checks corrected_t against an independent loop reference (references_ms6.corrected_repeated_t) to 1e-10, so the formula is certified; nothing in the repo simulates coverage or Type I error of the interval, which is the claim's substance ('approximately valid'). test_2_families_are_compared_on_repeated_kfold_whatever_validation_leads checks the 10 × 5 substrate and df 49 are used. The comment 'Bouckaert & Frank 2004: 10 × 10' beside COMPARISON_REPEATS=10 is accurate about the source, but the app's default K is 5, so the app runs 10 × 5. A known-truth null simulation (two identical families, 10 × 5, check ~5% rejection / 95% coverage of zero) would lift this to certified. Note: pytest is absent from .venv; tests were run with the repo's venv/bin/python.

source_note: Verified on rdrr.io (CRAN docs): randomForest ntree=500, mtry max(floor(p/3),1) for regression and floor(sqrt(p)) for classes, replace=TRUE, sampsize=nrow(x), nodesize 5 for regression ('Minimum size of terminal nodes'); ranger num.trees=500, mtry floor(sqrt(p)) for every forest, replace=TRUE, sample.fraction 1, min.node.size 10 for probability ('Minimal node size to split at'), min.bucket (terminal node) default 1. So the regression set is exactly randomForest's defaults and the class set is ranger's probability-forest defaults, with the leaf at 10 where ranger's 10 is the split size and its leaf minimum is 1. RECIPES §2.2 adopts these and states the scikit-learn bagging departure; forest.py:4-11 states the leaf-vs-node departure as 'stricter'. That the departure is 'acceptable' is the app's judgment, not in any cited source (RECIPES' tuning row cites Kruppa et al. 2014 on leaves near 10% of n for probability machines, which points the same way but is not a ruling on the default).
note: The test (7 parametrizations, passes) checks the resolved estimator parameters and the fitted trees' max_features_/min_samples_leaf against randomForest 4.x and ranger 0.18 usage text copied into the test; that text matches the live CRAN docs, so it is an independent provenance reference and would fail if the settings drifted. It certifies the 'are the defaults' part only. The 'stricter but acceptable' part is a stated judgment with no test or source: the app's own text says only 'stricter', so if this clause is shown, word it as a stated departure (a leaf of at least 10 rows where ranger splits nodes of 10 or more and allows leaves of 1), not as validated.

source_note: Internal: materiality_calibration.json 'invariance' (theorem 'Frisch–Waugh–Lovell'), SURFACING_POLICY §2.6 amendment and WAVE_C6A_PLAN §7 ruling 2 exist and give a methods reason (the model matrix's column space is unchanged, so the focal coefficient, its SE and fitted values do not move), not just a decision. Frisch & Waugh 1933 / Lovell 1963 establish this for least squares only. For logistic, Cox, GEE, mixed and survey fits the right basis is equivariance of the estimator (and of sandwich/Taylor variances, V → A⁻¹VA⁻ᵀ) under an invertible reparameterization, given an intercept or baseline hazard; no source for that is cited. Nothing cited covers multiple imputation, where the claim fails as 'exactly' (see note).
note: The named test fits statsmodels OLS directly (it does not import the engine's fit path) and shows the exposure's coefficient and classical SE equal to 1e-12 under male vs female coding. That is a valid check of the theorem for OLS but not of the app's reported numbers or of the claim's wider regime (any family, HC/cluster/survey SEs, MI-pooled). Counterexample found in the regime: under Estimate with multiple imputation, the relabeled column (no blanks) is still a predictor in the other columns' imputation models, and imputation._norm_draw (mice's norm) draws β* = β̂ + σ*·chol((XᵀX + 1e-5·diag)⁻¹)·z. Neither the diagonal ridge nor the Cholesky factor is equivariant under D → 1 − D. Read-only check with the engine's own _norm, same seed, n = 400, 20% blanks: the imputed values differed by up to 0.118 (residual SD 1). The _binary draws happened to agree in that run. So MI-pooled estimates and intervals move by Monte Carlo noise, and 'changes no reported number … needs no post-lock check' is not exact there. It holds in distribution only. adjustment_only() never checks the missing-data strategy. Smaller edges: an 'energy'-role column under the density or partition energy methods enters as a divisor or component, not as an additive term, so recoding would change the exposure (a two-valued energy column is unlikely, but the rule allows it). For OLS, likelihood families with an intercept, and their sandwich or Taylor variances, the claim is a standard result. Suggest excluding MI (and energy under non-additive methods) from rule 2, or restating it as 'unchanged in expectation; refit noise only', and citing reparameterization equivariance beside FWL.

source_note: No source is cited for strata. StratifiedEnergyAdjuster.estimand() (energy.py:1392-1396) returns METHOD_TABLE['residual']['estimand'] (energy.py:163-172), the pooled residual's sentence citing McCullough & Byrd 2023. That sentence holds for the pooled residual: N_adj = N − bE + const, so span(N_adj, E, 1) = span(N, E, 1). The stratified form is N_adj = N − b_s(E − Ē_s) − N̄_s + N̄ (energy.py:1166-1168). With level-specific slopes b_s, N_adj − N contains Σ_s 1[s]·b_s·E, a strata × energy term outside span(N, E, C, S). The pooled-residual source therefore does not cover this regime, and no ruling in the repo derives it for strata.
note: The app does rely on this claim: the stratified residual shows the pooled residual's estimand sentence ('the coefficient is the standard model's exactly'). The judged test compares the engine with an independent statsmodels fit of y ~ within-sex residual + energy + age + sex, not with the standard model y ~ N + E + C, so it would pass even if the claim were false. Read-only counterexample with the engine's StratifiedEnergyAdjuster: n = 2000, true slope of N on E 0.05 in one sex and 0.02 in the other, true model y = 0.3N + 0.01E + 2·sex. Standard-model coefficient 0.2985; stratified-residual coefficient with sex in the model 0.2918, and the same without sex. Even with equal true slopes, the sampled b_s differ and the coefficients differ (0.32451 vs 0.32474). The claim holds exactly only when every level uses the same slope (e.g. every level on the pooled slope) and the strata indicators are in the outcome model. Otherwise the estimand is the substitution effect with energy adjusted within strata (an energy-by-strata adjustment), close to the standard model's only when the slopes are similar. The estimand sentence should be stratum-specific.

source_note: CLINICAL_SURVEY_PACK.md (docs/turbotab-next/reference/research/, line 241-244), anti-pattern 1 'Complete-case by default … Flag when listwise deletion drops >10% of rows', exists and is quoted correctly. It is a decision with a reason (complete cases in clinically driven missingness are a selected subpopulation) but no evidence tag and no external source for the 10% figure. Unlike neighboring items it is not marked SETTLED or CONVENTION. The pack is an internal ruling, so it supports the decision but gives no methods basis for the threshold.
note: Code matches: ROW_LOSS_SHARE = 0.10 (missing.py:87); row_loss_concern fires when share > 0.10 (missing.py:1751-1768), from the complete_case branch of stages/modeling.py:1415-1420. The concern compares dropped and kept rows on the outcome and up to 4 predictors, by pooled-SD SMD for numbers and a two-proportion SMD on the kept rows' modal level for categories. The test_7 tests check the boundary (0.10 silent, above speaks) and the SMD arithmetic only; there is no truth to certify for a threshold. The on-screen text attributes the 10% to the pack without calling it a convention. Reword it as a convention ('a convention this app uses: more than 10% of rows lost'), and keep the existing caveat that complete cases are unbiased only if missingness does not depend on the outcome given the predictors. As the inventory notes, the kept-vs-dropped comparison can only show dependence on observed variables.

source_note: Verified on PMC (PMC2517157), Tooze et al. 2006 J Am Diet Assoc 106:1575: 'the WPM [within-person mean] method … includes within-person variability, the variance of usual intake is inflated'; 'The WPM method usually leads to biased estimates of the prevalence of either inadequate or excess food intake'; 'The within-person variation … does not contribute to long-term intake.' NUTRITION_PACK §03 (docs/turbotab-next/reference/research/NUTRITION_PACK.md:346-348) says 'Averaging 2 days leaves too much within-person variance in the distribution; the tails are too fat, so prevalence of both inadequacy and excess is over-estimated' [SETTLED], and line 795-797 says the same for the EAR cut-point. Tooze 2010 (amount-only) is cited for the model in methods/usual_intake.py; I did not fetch it.
note: Code: the mean_of_days option in usual_intake.py:435-441 is rank_lower under inference, labeled 'unsound for percentiles and prevalence: the tails are too fat; shown only beside the usual-intake distribution, labeled'; not offered under prediction. The test uses a known-truth simulation (simulate_amount, hand-coded in the test file, 200 datasets of 1,000 people). It would fail if the mean-of-days 10th percentile were not more than 15% below the true usual-intake 10th percentile, if single days were not lower still, or if the NCI fit missed the truth by more than 1.5%. It checks the lower tail only. The upper tail and the share-below-cut-off for the mean-of-days distribution are not asserted, so the 'both tails' half rests on Tooze 2006 and the variance identity σ²_b + σ²_w/k > σ²_b. Also, in the fixture 30% of people have one recall, so their 'mean of recalls' is a single day.

source_note: Verified on Europe PMC: Bland & Altman, J Biopharm Stat 2007;17(4):571-582 (methods for repeated pairs 'when the underlying quantity is assumed to be changing'), and Zou, Stat Methods Med Res 2013;22:630-642 (MOVER confidence intervals for LoA with multiple observations; 'A fixed number of replicates per individual is not needed'). The ANOVA components with λ = (n² − Σm_i²)/((k−1)n) are B&A's 'true value varies' form. The repo's R reference in test_d5 codes Zou's own form (person-means variance s̄² and harmonic mean m_h). With equal m_i the two coincide, and the test shows it. With unequal m_i the app runs MOVER on B&A's MS_b/λ + (1 − 1/λ)·MS_w, a hybrid of B&A's components and Zou's MOVER, not Zou's unbalanced procedure, though Zou does cover unbalanced data. The inventory's 'MOVER on unbalanced data is the app's extension' is therefore only partly right: Zou handles unbalanced data, but in a different way. I did not read the full texts, so the bias-variance formula and t(k−1) are checked against the R reference, not against either paper.
note: Code at agreement.py:418-468 matches the statement term for term, including the truncation branch (se = √(var(person means)/k)) and a concern sentence when it fires. Tests run here: all 3 pass, with R available. The balanced test compares against R's aov mean squares and an independent R coding of Zou 2013's MOVER (s̄², m_h) to 1e-10, so it would fail if the components or the MOVER limits were wrong. Its SimplyAgree branch is skipped here because the package is not installed. The unbalanced test compares the components with aov, but its MOVER reference recodes the app's own λ-form by hand, so it is an implementation pin for the hybrid, not an independent check of Zou's unbalanced method. The truncation test checks the person-means SE against a hand computation. Show the unbalanced case as 'B&A 2007 components with Zou's MOVER', or switch to Zou's own unbalanced form.

corrected_statement: By a stated convention (by analogy with the 100-event rule for binary outcomes, which is cited), the app takes 100 held-out rows for a continuous outcome, and 100 held-out rows in the rarest class or level for a multiclass or ordinal outcome, as the floor for a useful held-out score. When a 20% holdout falls below it, 'Cross-validation only' is offered first, and every holdout option stays on offer.
source_note: seal.py:668-687 sets SealFloor(convention=True, source=None) for regression, multiclass and ordinal. The binary and time-to-event floors cite Collins, Ogundimu & Altman 2016 and Vergouwe et al. 2005, which are about events in external validation of binary or survival models, not rows of a continuous outcome. The extension is the app's analogy. No internal ruling gives a methods reason for 100 rows beyond the analogy. The neighboring precision note, an R² SE of 2√R²(1−R²)/√n at R² = 0.2, gives about ±0.14 at n = 100 and is a better stated reason, but it is not used to set the floor. Literature on minimum sizes for validating continuous outcomes (e.g. Archer et al. 2021) is not cited.
note: The statement drops the app's own framing. The app says 'A convention: at least 100 held-out rows, by analogy with the 100-event rule', and the claim restates that as a fact ('needs … to be useful'). Mechanics are as stated: measure() flags n_holdout < 100 for regression and the rarest held-out class or level < 100 for multiclass and ordinal, and holdout_options() moves 'Cross-validation only' first when the 20% option is below the floor. On screen it is already worded as a convention, so it can stay as it is; do not promote it to a cited rule. There is no test of whether 100 rows gives a useful score, and none is needed for a convention.

corrected_statement: A column with at most one distinct non-missing value is settled as excluded at high confidence without asking, and is shown as 'every row holds the same value'. This includes a column that holds one value on some rows and blanks on the rest. Only a column with no blanks has no variation for a model to use; a one-value-plus-blank column varies through its blanks.
source_note: The basis is the KIND_RULES text 'a constant has no variation for any model to use' (readings.py:1172-1174), an internal statement with no source. For a strictly constant column none is needed: it is collinear with the intercept, and no tree can split on it.
note: The grade covers the strict case only (a column truly constant on every row), where the claim is trivially true. The app's test ignores blanks: constant_values() uses _present() = dropna() (readings.py:425-428, 838-843), and stages/rows.py:591 tests n_unique ≤ 1, where datastore's n_unique counts non-missing values only. A read-only probe showed constant_values(['yes', None, None, 'yes', None]) and constant_values([1.0, NaN, 1.0]) both return settles=True, value='excluded', evidence='every row holds the same value'. That evidence is false when blanks exist. It also drops a checkbox-style 'yes'/blank column that encodes a binary (or a missing-indicator signal under Predict) without asking. The judged test only checks that the rule does not settle a normal predictor (a 50-value normal draw) and that it settles [3.0]×40; it has no one-value-plus-blank fixture, so it would not catch this. Suggest: settle only when there are also no blanks; otherwise ask, or read the column as value-vs-blank.

corrected_statement: For NHANES tables the app offers first the weight its least-common-denominator rule names. An OGTT analyte (LBXGLT/LBDGLTSI, or any variable recorded only on WTSOG* rows) gets the OGTT subsample weight. A fasting analyte (glucose, triglycerides, LDL, insulin, apoB by name, or any variable recorded only on WTSAF* rows) gets the fasting subsample weight. Any column whose name starts DR1T/DR2T/DR1I/DR2I/DR1_/DR2_/DRXT gets the day-1 dietary weight, or the two-day weight when day-2 recall variables are present and the table has it; the same applies to DBQ/DBD diet-behavior questionnaire columns, which are interview variables, not recalls. Otherwise the MEC examination weight is named whenever it is in the table, even when every variable comes from the household interview, and the interview weight only when no MEC weight is present. A variable recorded only where a subsample weight is positive (at most 1% of its rows outside, missing on at least 5% of the table, at least 10 rows; the app's own tolerances) is read as that subsample's. Unknown or unconfirmed subsample weights leave the choice to the user. The named weight comes first, then the weights of the samples that contain it.
source_note: Verified on the CDC NHANES Weighting tutorial (wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/tutorials/weighting.aspx): 'You must use the weight of the smallest subpopulation that includes all the variables …'; the 'least common denominator' rule of thumb; fasting triglycerides → 'fasting subsample weights (wtsaf4yr)'; MEC data → 'MEC exam weight'; first-day recall → wtdrd1; both days → wtdr2d. The tutorial also says interview-only analyses use the interview weight (wtint4yr), which the code does not do when a MEC weight is present (recognizers.py:1982-1987: rank 1 if present). The CDC DBQ_J documentation says most DBQ items were asked in the home, and that the exam weight applies when they are joined to MEC data. Neither source supports treating DBQ/DBD as day-1 dietary-weight variables (_DIETARY_VARIABLE, recognizers.py:1817). The tutorial says nothing on combining dietary and fasting variables; the app's choice of the fasting weight there follows LCD reasoning but is not stated by the source. SUBSAMPLE_SLACK, MIN_MISSING and MIN_ROWS are labeled TurboTab's own tolerances.
note: The tests hand-specify the tutorial's expected weight for fixed fixtures (fasting → WTSAF2YR, pre-pandemic → WTSAFPRP, OGTT → WTSOG2YR, no fasting → dietary). They would catch a misapplication in those cases, but not if the rule itself were wrong, and they have no fixture for interview-only variables or DBQ columns. The departures from the source are conservative, not biasing. A MEC weight for interview-only variables, or a dietary weight for DBQ-only variables, restricts the analysis to a smaller weighted sample, which is valid but loses rows, and in the interview-only case contradicts the tutorial's explicit example. Worth fixing: drop DBQ/DBD from _DIETARY_VARIABLE, and offer WTINT first when no variable is an exam, lab or dietary one (or ask).

source_note: BLUEPRINT §14.2 ('Ask, don't guess', Nolan 2026-10-03; docs/turbotab-next/BLUEPRINT.md:593-612) exists. It is a procedural ruling (confirm readings that feed a number-changing consumer, in one block), not a methods reason. The methods content, that a batch label is nominal and so must enter as a factor and not as a slope on its numeric code, is the standard way batch is adjusted as a covariate (the app cites Nygaard, Rødland & Hovig 2016, 'account for batch in the statistical analysis', for the covariate answer). It is definitional rather than something a source needs to establish, and none is cited for it here.
note: Code (batch.py:767-784): under method 'covariate' it refuses with batch_covariate_unsettled when the batch column's role is not settled as covariate, or when its dtype is numeric/integer and code_or_count is not confirmed 'code'. The exit is one confirm_readings block. A text-typed batch needs only the role. test_5c pins the refusal, its two items and acceptance once both are settled. It does not check that the confirmed batch then enters the model matrix as indicators, so it would not catch a code column still entering as one slope. The on-screen 'one indicator per batch' is loose: with an intercept and reference coding there are K − 1 indicators. This is low-risk procedural gating.

corrected_statement: The teaching card states, badged CONVENTION (CLINICAL_SURVEY_PACK §A5.5), that bootstrap optimism correction is the recommended default for internal validation, repeated cross-validation is acceptable, and a single train/test split is the weakest option at typical clinical sample sizes. The app applies this order only under prediction, without time order, below 20,000 units (validation.RESAMPLE_BELOW, from Harrell 2017). Families that nearly memorize their rows (boosted trees, random forest) are exempt: they keep their cross-validated score because the bootstrap overstates them. At or above 20,000 units one k-fold run leads, and under inference or time order k-fold leads.
source_note: CLINICAL_SURVEY_PACK.md §A5.5 (docs/turbotab-next/reference/research/, lines 634-638) says it verbatim: 'Bootstrap optimism correction is the recommended default (it uses all the data and has smaller variance than a single split); repeated k-fold CV is acceptable. A single train/test split is the weakest option and is discouraged at typical clinical sample sizes.' It is tagged '[… the bootstrap-vs-CV preference is CONVENTION]'. That is an internal ruling with a brief methods reason. External backing, verified on Europe PMC: Steyerberg, Harrell et al., J Clin Epidemiol 2001;54:774-781, on logistic regression: split-sample 'gave overly pessimistic estimates of performance, with large variability'; they 'recommend bootstrapping for estimation of internal validity of a predictive logistic regression model'. validation.py also cites Harrell 2017 (split-val blog) for the 20,000 threshold. The card cites only the pack, not these.
note: The ordering is implemented in models/validation.py:validation_plan (lines 404-429) and read by seal.py. 'Typical clinical sample sizes' is undefined on the card; in code it is n_units < 20,000. The primary evidence (Steyerberg 2001) is for logistic regression. For flexible learners the app itself holds that the bootstrap overstates performance (bootstrap_optimism = False for boosted trees and forests, with a replication in test_wp9), so the card's unconditional 'recommended default' is broader than the app's practice. Suggest the card add 'for regression models' or name the tree exception, and cite Steyerberg 2001 beside the pack.

source_note: Verified on the CDC NHANES Variance Estimation tutorial (wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/tutorials/VarianceEstimation.aspx): 'you should never delete or drop records from your analysis dataset before executing your analysis procedures' (deleting fixes the random subpopulation sizes within PSUs and underestimates SEs); 'NCHS recommends the use of the Taylor Series Linearization methods'; PSUs 'can be treated as sampling with replacement because the sampling fraction … is small'; 'Degrees of freedom = number of PSUs − number of strata'. The domain-specific df rule (only strata and PSUs holding the subgroup's rows) is quoted in models/survey.py:38-42 from Analytic Guidelines 2011–2016 §3.2.3.2. I fetched the guidelines PDF but could not extract its text here, so that sentence and the section number are checked only against the repo's quote.
note: The test passes here. Through the server it compares the domain fit's coefficients and SEs with samplics (independent; weights zeroed outside the domain, as R's subset() does) and with a definitional Taylor-linearization reference, both to 1e-9. It checks df = 8 by the NCHS rule (20 domain PSUs − 12 strata) and shows that deleting the rows gives a different design (samplics refuses its lonely strata, and the deleted-file SE differs by more than 2%). It would fail if the engine deleted rows, used the full-design df, or linearized differently. As the inventory notes, deleting rows does not always change SEs materially. The domain df rule is NCHS's convention; Korn & Graubard and Lumley discuss alternatives.

corrected_statement: BEATS_PREDICT §9 ruling 3 (a design ruling, planned as P27, status NEW) says internal–external cross-validation across survey cycles should be summarized by random-effects meta-analysis of the log MSE, with an HKSJ interval and a t(k − 2) prediction interval. The engine does not do this today. validation.internal_external pools the primary score per cluster with performance.random_effects: DerSimonian–Laird τ², a normal-z confidence interval, a prediction interval on t(k − 2) when k ≥ 3, on the identity scale (logit only for AUC). The REML + HKSJ pooling in methods/site_validation.py is not wired into the fit (INBOX T3). The '24.4 to 42.0' prediction interval appears only in the design document's worked example.
source_note: Verified on Europe PMC: IntHout, Ioannidis & Borm, BMC Med Res Methodol 2014;14 ('HKSJ … consistently results in more adequate error rates than the DL method, especially when the number of studies is small'), which supports HKSJ over DL. Snell et al., Stat Methods Med Res 2018;27:3505-3522, cited 'on choosing the scale', studies only the C-statistic, calibration slope, calibration-in-the-large and E/O, recommending logit C and log E/O. It does not address the MSE, so it does not support the log-MSE scale. Higgins, Thompson & Spiegelhalter 2009 (the t(k − 2) prediction interval) and Riley et al. 2016 (IECV) were not fetched; they are standard for the prediction interval and the IECV design. The reason for the log scale (on the identity scale, cycles with larger MSE have larger SEs, correlation 0.81, so less weight, which is optimistic) is the design owner's own observation on this dataset, not a sourced rule.
test_judged: turbotab/core/tests/acceptance/test_site_validation.py::test_reml_with_hksj_and_the_riley_interval_match_metafor (tests the unwired REML/HKSJ pooling core against metafor; nothing tests a log-MSE IECV summary, which the engine does not compute)
note: The claim describes a design ruling for a feature not yet built; the app's computed summary is materially different (DL, z interval, identity scale). If the user-facing '24.4 to 42.0 (95% prediction interval)' were shown now, it would not come from the engine. The engine's identity-scale result in the same document is 31.8 with a prediction interval of 23.7 to 38.2 (BEATS_PREDICT.md:1416). Before shipping P27, decide the scale with a reason that does not lean on Snell 2018, which says nothing about MSE. A log-scale RMSE/MSE needs a delta-method SE (se/MSE). Also wire site_validation's metafor-checked REML/HKSJ instead of keeping two summaries (INBOX T3). With k = 8 cycles, τ² is imprecise, and HKSJ helps the CI but not the prediction interval's reliance on τ̂.
